newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS - U.S. air travel seen firm but not jet prices.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - U.S. air travel seen firm but not jet prices.

text.p: A robust U.S. air travel market should translate into a healthy rise in demand for jet fuel this year, but airlines are expected to get a break on prices, according to industry experts.

Jet fuel consumption by the 41 largest U.S. international and national carriers is forecast to increase 2.2 percent to 17.8 billion gallons this year from 17.4 billion gallons in 1996, according to David Swierenga, economist with the Air Transport Association of America, an industry trade group.
Analysts said the higher demand forecast is based on a rising number of departures as well a modest jump in the average flight length.
Swierenga said he expected 1997 departures in the U.S. to rise about 2.5 percent and trip distance from 999 miles to 1,004 miles.
"The reason the mileage average would increase is because of the large number of international flights," said Stephen Klein, analyst with Standard & Poor's Equity Group.
"We've also seen faster growth at the shorter-hop airlines," Klein said. "And they claim to be taking share away from automobiles" rather than the larger airlines, he added.

Despite rising demand jet fuel prices are widely forecast to moderate this year, especially compared with the sharply higher prices seen late last year when surcharges of up to three percent were added by the largest airlines after fuel prices surged 50 percent in just three months.
Jet fuel prices, which typically make up between 10 and 15 percent of an carrier's costs, follow heating oil and crude prices, both of which have been falling sharply since the start of the year.
Swierenga forecast prices paid for jet fuel would fall to between 62 to 63 cents per gallon in 1997 compared to 65.4 cents paid by the largest airlines in 1996.

Crude oil prices fell from a post-Gulf War high of $26.74 a barrel (New York Mercantile Exchange futures) in early January to a low of $18.96 by early April. And heating oil prices also have declined amid a much milder winter than in 1995/1996.
In recent weeks, most airlines serving the North Atlantic and Latin American routes have eliminated the cargo fuel surcharges that were implemented in the autumn.
"We see (fuel) costs bouncing back up in the second quarter, but tapering off after that and through the rest of the year," said Jeffrey Long, airline industry analyst for J.P. Morgan.

Long said he expected wholesale jet fuel prices in the active U.S. Gulf of Mexico market to rebound a bit in the second quarter after falling more than 20 percent since the start of the year. But then he expects a resumption of the slide through the rest of the year.

Brian Harris, Lehman Brothers' airline analyst also said he expects lower jet fuel prices, running around three percent below last year in the second quarter, eight percent below in the third quarter and 12 percent lower in the fourth quarter.
However, analysts say that whether airlines pass on any cost savings to passengers will depend on whether they locked in prices when they were high or rode them out.
